title: Semiconductor industry and market-structure field guide
description: A maintained reference for mapping the semiconductor value chain, its operating economics, and the market signals that matter. Update stable concepts here; put dated developments in each day's research file.
source_hierarchy: Company filings, earnings releases, and investor-relations materials for company-specific figures and guidance.
WSTS and SIA for published industry sales and forecast series; preserve each source's scope and vintage.
SEMI for equipment, fab capacity, and materials context; distinguish orders, billings, and shipments.
Government export-control, subsidy, and trade publications for policy facts.
News headlines for discovery and attribution only until claims are confirmed in primary sources.

chain_stages.name: Architecture, IP & chip design
chain_stages.description: Companies define chip architecture, license reusable IP, and design products for specific workloads. Fabless firms outsource wafer production; some integrated device makers (IDMs) also fabricate chips.
chain_stages.economics: R&D, software ecosystems, product mix, design wins, and customer concentration shape returns. A design win is not the same as a shipped unit or recognized revenue.
watch: Product launches and benchmark-qualified performance per watt
Customer qualification, design-win conversion, and revenue concentration
R&D intensity, gross margin, and inventory
chain_stages.risk: Roadmaps, software lock-in, export rules, customer-funded development, and rapid substitution can change the addressable market.

chain_stages.name: Wafer fabrication: foundries and IDMs
chain_stages.description: Foundries sell manufacturing capacity to external customers; IDMs design and manufacture their own products and may also sell foundry services.
chain_stages.economics: Revenue depends on wafer starts, node and product mix, utilization, yields, and wafer pricing. Capacity is capital intensive and takes years to plan and qualify.
watch: Capex and capacity plans by node and geography
Utilization, wafer pricing, yield commentary, and customer prepayments
Depreciation, cash flow, and node-specific demand
chain_stages.risk: High fixed costs amplify utilization changes. Announced capacity, installed equipment, qualified capacity, and customer-usable output are different milestones.

chain_stages.name: Wafer-fab equipment, process control & materials
chain_stages.description: Lithography, deposition, etch, inspection, metrology, process-control tools, and specialty materials enable wafer production.
chain_stages.economics: Tool intensity, replacement cycles, installed-base service revenue, customer capex, and export licensing drive orders and margins.
watch: Bookings, billings, backlog, cancellations, and book-to-bill definitions
Foundry and memory capex by customer and node
Service revenue and export-license exposure
chain_stages.risk: Backlog can shift or be cancelled; a tool shipment is not equivalent to productive wafer capacity.

chain_stages.name: Memory: DRAM, NAND and high-bandwidth memory
chain_stages.description: Memory is often sold into cyclical markets. HBM uses stacked DRAM and advanced packaging to meet bandwidth and power requirements for accelerators.
chain_stages.economics: Bit supply growth, utilization, yields, inventory, contract pricing, product mix, and capex interact. HBM has different qualification and packaging constraints than commodity memory.
watch: DRAM, NAND, and HBM pricing separately
Supplier inventory, customer inventory, and inventory days
HBM capacity, yields, qualification, and packaging allocation
chain_stages.risk: Strong pricing or HBM demand does not establish that all memory products are tight or that current margins are durable.

chain_stages.name: Advanced packaging, substrates & OSAT
chain_stages.description: Foundries and outsourced semiconductor assembly and test (OSAT) providers assemble dies, interposers, substrates, and memory into finished packages.
chain_stages.economics: Package complexity, substrate availability, thermal design, test time, yields, and qualified capacity can constrain system shipments even when wafer supply is available.
watch: Advanced-packaging capacity and customer allocation
Substrate lead times, yields, and test bottlenecks
Wafer-to-package-to-system shipment conversion
chain_stages.risk: A reported packaging bottleneck is product- and customer-specific; distinguish capacity plans from qualified output.

chain_stages.name: Distribution, systems & end markets
chain_stages.description: Distributors, contract manufacturers, and system companies turn components into servers, phones, vehicles, industrial controls, and other end products.
chain_stages.economics: Sell-in to channels can diverge from sell-through to end users. Design wins, system build plans, and finished-goods inventory help reconcile demand with chip shipments.
watch: End-market unit volumes and system build plans
Distributor and customer inventory, cancellations, and lead times
Sell-in versus sell-through and revenue-recognition timing
chain_stages.risk: A supply-chain order is not always final demand; double ordering and inventory digestion can reverse quickly.

market_mechanics.name: Inventory and cycle
market_mechanics.mechanism: A long, capital-intensive supply chain can overshoot demand. Orders, distributor inventory, customer inventory, fab utilization, and spot/contract prices turn at different times.
watch: Company and channel inventory in dollars and days
Sequential and year-over-year sales, with seasonality stated
Utilization, lead times, cancellations, and pricing by product
market_mechanics.pitfall: Do not treat one company's inventory or a headline shipment forecast as a sector-wide cycle measure.

market_mechanics.name: Capacity, yield and bottlenecks
market_mechanics.mechanism: Nominal wafer capacity is only useful when the process, yield, packaging, testing, and customer qualification are ready for a particular product.
watch: Capex versus depreciation and installed capacity
Yield and qualification milestones
Constraint location: wafer, HBM, packaging, substrate, power, or system integration
market_mechanics.pitfall: A bottleneck can migrate; adding capacity at one stage may not raise system shipments.

market_mechanics.name: Contracting, allocation and customer concentration
market_mechanics.mechanism: Long-term agreements, prepayments, allocation, take-or-pay terms, and concentrated buyers can shape visibility, pricing power, and downside if plans change.
watch: Backlog and remaining performance obligations definitions
Customer concentration and cancellation terms in filings
Prepayments, commitments, and cash-conversion cycle
market_mechanics.pitfall: Backlog and announced orders are not guaranteed revenue; compare contract terms, delivery timing, and recognized sales.

market_mechanics.name: ETF concentration, breadth and index flows
market_mechanics.mechanism: Semiconductor benchmarks can be concentrated in a small set of large companies. Index weights, rebalances, creations/redemptions, and benchmark demand can influence constituent flows.
watch: ETF holdings and weight changes from issuer files
Equal-weight versus cap-weight performance and constituent breadth
Fund creations/redemptions and benchmark rebalances
market_mechanics.pitfall: Price × share volume is not ETF flow; market capitalization is not liquidity; headline breadth is not causal attribution.

market_mechanics.name: Options positioning and dealer hedging
market_mechanics.mechanism: Options hedging may amplify or dampen short-horizon moves depending on dealer inventory, strike, expiry, and underlying price changes.
watch: Open interest and volume by strike/expiry
Implied volatility and skew versus realized volatility
Timestamped, methodology-disclosed dealer gamma estimates
market_mechanics.pitfall: Open interest does not reveal who is long or short; vendor gamma estimates are model-dependent and should not be stated as observed dealer positions.

market_mechanics.name: Liquidity, volatility and rates
market_mechanics.mechanism: Highly valued growth equities can react to real rates, earnings revisions, volatility, and liquidity conditions. Intraday execution costs depend on spread, depth, and volatility.
watch: Real yields and broad risk appetite alongside sector returns
Bid-ask spread, depth, turnover, and volatility from timestamped market data
Earnings revisions and valuation against growth assumptions
market_mechanics.pitfall: Daily closes and free quote volume cannot measure order-book depth, market impact, or the cause of a price move.

market_mechanics.name: Policy and geographic concentration
market_mechanics.mechanism: Export controls, subsidies, tariffs, and restrictions on equipment or end-customer access alter addressable demand, location choices, and supply-chain economics.
watch: Primary government text and effective dates
Company-specific revenue exposure and license status
Capex location, construction progress, and customer qualification
market_mechanics.pitfall: Separate enacted rules from proposals, reported discussions, and company-specific exemptions.

glossary.definition: A chip designer that outsources most or all wafer fabrication to foundries.
glossary.signal: Track product mix, design wins, outsourced wafer availability, and customer concentration.

glossary.definition: A manufacturer that fabricates wafers for external customers; some firms also design their own products.
glossary.signal: Track capacity and utilization by node, customer, yield, and wafer pricing.

glossary.definition: An integrated device manufacturer that designs and manufactures some of its own chips.
glossary.signal: Separate internal manufacturing economics from any external foundry business.

glossary.definition: Outsourced semiconductor assembly and test provider.
glossary.signal: Track packaging mix, test capacity, substrate access, and qualification.

glossary.definition: A wafer entering a fabrication process; it is not yet a completed wafer or shippable chip.
glossary.signal: Compare starts with cycle time, yield, and completed-unit demand.

glossary.definition: The proportion of process output meeting required specifications; definitions vary by stage and product.
glossary.signal: Yield improvements can increase saleable output without an equivalent increase in wafer starts.

glossary.definition: High-bandwidth memory built from vertically stacked DRAM dies and integrated with advanced packaging.
glossary.signal: Check product-specific supply, qualification, yields, and packaging capacity.

glossary.definition: Extreme ultraviolet lithography used for selected advanced patterning steps.
glossary.signal: Tool delivery, installation, qualification, and productive utilization are separate milestones.

glossary.definition: A ratio of orders received to products billed over a stated period; industry definitions and coverage matter.
glossary.signal: Read the source's period, geography, product scope, and revisions.

glossary.definition: Inventory held by distributors and sometimes downstream customers, distinct from supplier inventory.
glossary.signal: Use company-specific definitions and days-of-inventory context; do not aggregate incompatible scopes.

glossary.definition: Sell-in is supplier shipment into a channel; sell-through is a channel's sale to the next buyer or end user.
glossary.signal: A gap can indicate channel build or drawdown rather than end-demand acceleration.

glossary.definition: Packaging approaches that combine dies or connect them with dense interconnects, including chiplets and 2.5D/3D integration.
glossary.signal: Map each claimed constraint to a specific package, supplier, qualification, and date.
